source_title: WeWork Inc. Form 10-Q for quarterly period ended June 30, 2023 (going-concern disclosure)
publisher_issuer: WeWork Inc. (filed with U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission); corroborated by CNBC, NPR, TechCrunch coverage of the August 2023 going-concern disclosure and November 2023 Chapter 11 filing
company_context: WeWork is a flexible-workspace / coworking platform that scaled to billions in annual revenue but never reached sustained profitability. In its Q2 2023 10-Q (released August 8, 2023) it disclosed substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern despite high revenue, and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on November 6, 2023. SUBSTITUTION NOTE: used in place of a pure-software SaaS because it is the strongest documented case of a high-revenue, recurring-membership growth company hitting an explicit going-concern/cash crisis with primary SEC disclosure.
business_type: Asset-heavy, recurring-membership flexible workspace platform; long-term lease liabilities against shorter-term member revenue, structurally negative free cash flow
company_size_stage: large public company (formerly ~$47B peak private valuation), high-revenue but unprofitable
time_period: Q2 2023 (quarter ended June 30, 2023) through Chapter 11 filing November 6, 2023
macro_context: Post-pandemic office-demand shift, elevated interest rates raising refinancing cost, and rising member churn pressuring a heavily lease-encumbered model.
outcome_category: 7 - high revenue but cash crisis / going concern
evidence_summary: WeWork reported Q2 2023 consolidated revenue of about $844 million (up about 4% year over year) yet disclosed, as a result of losses, projected cash needs, and rising member churn combined with current liquidity levels, that substantial doubt existed about its ability to continue as a going concern. As of June 30, 2023 it held about $205 million in cash and cash equivalents and about $680 million in total liquidity. The net loss for the quarter was about $397 million. The company filed for Chapter 11 on November 6, 2023, reporting about $18.65 billion in total debts against about $15.06 billion in total assets. This is a high-revenue company whose binding constraint was liquidity and lease obligations, not lack of sales.
owner_decision_context: Management had pursued rapid lease-funded expansion to grow revenue and valuation, leaving the company with large long-term lease liabilities that, combined with churn and high rates, outran available liquidity.
action_taken: Disclosed going-concern doubt in August 2023, pursued lease restructuring and a debt-restructuring agreement with about 92% of lenders, and ultimately filed Chapter 11 in November 2023 to renegotiate or reject leases.
outcome_evidence: About $844 million quarterly revenue alongside only about $205 million cash and an explicit going-concern statement, followed by a November 6, 2023 Chapter 11 filing with debts of about $18.65 billion, confirm a high-revenue liquidity/solvency crisis rather than a demand failure.
